transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-12-02
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Aaron Chen (AE), Priya Nair (SE), Jules Park (CSM) - Redwood; Mark Diaz (SRE), Samantha Liu (Head of AI), Tomás Alvarez (Eng Manager) - Orion Health

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): Discussed root cause of latency spike on 2025-11-28; KV cache eviction and autoscaler interplay suspected; temporary mitigations reduced error rates; agreed on focussed reliability work and communication plan.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Aaron Chen: hey everybody, thanks for joining, um, appreciate you squeezing this in. we wanted to walk through the postmortem for the 11/28 degradation and make sure owners and next steps are clear. 
[00:11] Mark Diaz: yeah thanks Aaron. we had a pretty visible impact during our evening window, latency jumped and some requests timed out. we filed a P0 and your team was responsive, thanks for that.
[00:22] Samantha Liu: hi all. real quick — high level for us: patient-facing triage was delayed, so we need both the technical root cause and a communication plan for executives.
[00:30] Aaron Chen: understood. quick agenda — timeline recap, what we saw in the runtime, mitigations taken, proposed permanent fixes, then owners. sound ok?
[00:38] Tomás Alvarez: yep, let's do it.
[00:40] Priya Nair: quick note — we have a short kernel trace and the KV cache metrics; i'll share the charts after this call.
[00:46] Mark Diaz: that would help.

[02:05] Aaron Chen: ok timeline from our side: at 23:06 UTC on 11/28 we observed increased tail latency for the hosted inference path serving your production model, roughly 3x baseline p95, with a subset of requests hitting timeouts. around the same time autoscaler kicked more pods but we saw uneven CPU utilization.
[02:28] Priya Nair: adding — the serving runtime's kernel selector moved to a fallback code path for long sequences; that, combined with cold KV cache state after a surge, contributed to higher per-token compute. it's subtle but real.
[02:45] Samantha Liu: can you explain the KV cache thing in plain words?
[02:52] Priya Nair: sure — the KV cache stores key/value past tokens so decoding is faster on repeated conversations. when the cache gets evicted or misses spike, the system re-computes more which increases work per request. if many requests are cold it amplifies latency.
[03:10] Mark Diaz: yeah and from our traces it looked like there was a pronounced eviction wave — we saw cache TTLs shrink and a lot of small sessions reloading the model context.

[05:00] Aaron Chen: there were two interrelated contributors we believe: first, a bug in the autoscaler config that allowed aggressive downscaling after a brief lull, and second, a kernel selection heuristic that didn't favor the optimized path for the specific sequence-length distribution from your workload. both increased tail latency.
[05:24] Tomás Alvarez: autoscaler bug? can you be specific?
[05:28] Priya Nair: it's a config threshold — the scale-down grace window was too short, so after the burst finished, instances were removed before the cache warmed back up. when traffic returned, we were rebuilding caches in parallel leading to hotspots.
[05:45] Tomás Alvarez: got it. that explains a lot.

[07:10] Samantha Liu: were there any authentication or encryption delays? we saw some KMS timeouts in our sidecar logs.
[07:18] Aaron Chen: good callout — we saw transient KMS retries during the same window. looks like a separate but compounding issue: a brief elevated KMS latency caused some startup operations (key access) to retry which prolonged instance readiness.
[07:33] Mark Diaz: that was significant — several pods were in Init longer than usual. we correlate that with the autoscaler reaction.

[09:00] Aaron Chen: immediate mitigations we applied: increased scale-up and scale-down grace windows, disabled an experimental kernel heuristic, and enabled aggressive prefix caching for your tenant to reduce cold-cache penalties. we also opened a ticket with KMS team to review latency spike.
[09:22] Priya Nair: note: the prefix caching is safe but increases memory footprint slightly; we boxed it for Orion only.
[09:30] Tomás Alvarez: fine tradeoff for us — memory vs latency is acceptable.

[12:00] Mark Diaz: thanks. from our side we rotated SSO certs and rechecked our sidecar config; nothing else abnormal.

[14:15] Priya Nair: the kernel traces show a misclassification of byte-level sequence lengths — the compiler picked a conservative kernel which is slower for medium-length sequences. it's an edge case in our kernel-selection table; we'll push a fix to prefer the faster kernel for sequences in the 512-1500 token band.
[14:40] Aaron Chen: that change should give you a consistent p95 improvement without affecting other customers.

[17:00] Samantha Liu: are there any risks to that kernel change? regression risk?
[17:07] Priya Nair: low risk — we have unit perf tests but we'll run a canary on dedicated infra first. we'll also keep the old path as fallback for 48 hours post-deploy.

[19:40] Tomás Alvarez: we discussed private deployment as a risk reduction option. do we have an approximate timeline / blockers?
[19:48] Aaron Chen: short answer: feasible. blockers are network onboarding, KMS integration, and data residency requirements. Priya can lead a feasibility scoping session.
[19:57] Priya Nair: yes i'll prepare a checklist and a technical pre-req doc. we should also evaluate whether Dedicated reserved capacity addresses the eviction pattern without full private deployment.

[22:10] Mark Diaz: what about observability — during the incident we lacked some token-level traces. can we get more granular audit logs?
[22:19] Jules Park: absolutely. we can increase retention for your token trace and add a dashboard with request-id waterfall. need to align on retention window due to cost.
[22:30] Mark Diaz: propose 14 days for full traces, 90 days aggregated metrics.

[24:00] Aaron Chen: on SLA and credits — Jules will follow up offline with a draft calculation; we committed to a partial credit but the legal team wanted a documented timeline first.

[26:15] Samantha Liu: can you confirm SOC2/ISO logs were intact? that matters for our risk office.
[26:22] Aaron Chen: yes, audit logs were preserved and are available; we will include those in the redacted bundle. KMS access logs will also be included.

[28:00] Tomás Alvarez: ok what about an automated fallback routing policy? if latency exceeds threshold we want traffic to route to a warm dedicated pool or to a smaller faster quantized model to preserve availability.
[28:14] Priya Nair: we can implement a policy: primary -> warm dedicated pool -> quantized variant -> degrade politely. that would require model variants and routing policy configured; we can prototype in a week.

[30:40] Mark Diaz: threading that into our incident runbooks would be useful — trigger thresholds, who pages, and automatic mitigation steps.
[30:47] Jules Park: agree; we'll collaborate on runbook edits and give you a versioned document.

[33:10] Aaron Chen: quick interruption — there may be small transcription errors in the auto notes; "KV cash" sometimes appears in our logs, ignore that, it's KV cache.
[33:20] Samantha Liu: haha noted.

[34:50] Priya Nair: next technical steps from Redwood: 1) push kernel-selection fix to canary (internal) 2) extend scale grace windows on your tenant 3) enable prefix caching 4) add eviction-rate alerting. we'll report back with metrics pre/post.
[35:08] Tomás Alvarez: please include the synthetic QPS profile you used for the test.

[37:30] Mark Diaz: on our side we'll provide the sanitized request logs and the incident timeline with customer impact notes for legal.

[39:10] Aaron Chen: agreed. also FYI we'll include a small postmortem deck for execs summarizing cause, impact, remediation, and credits. Jules will draft and share.
[39:22] Jules Park: i'll share a draft by Friday (2025-12-05).

[41:00] Samantha Liu: what is the ask on on-prem? we need a list of security controls and estimated infra footprint.
[41:08] Priya Nair: i'll include a pre-req doc: network, firewall rules, KMS/HSM connectivity options, required GPUs and storage. also a timeline estimate ~4-8 weeks for a guarded pilot with network approvals.

[43:30] Tomás Alvarez: sounds good. any cost delta roughly for dedicated vs private?
[43:36] Aaron Chen: short: Dedicated reserved capacity is cheaper to start and faster to stand up; private has additional legal/compliance overhead and one-time onboarding fees. we'll include a PO-level estimate in the doc.

[45:10] Mark Diaz: one last thing — can we get a direct contact for on-call during these rollouts? someone we can escalate to if we see regression after kernel change?
[45:18] Aaron Chen: yes, Priya will be the escalation SE for the kernel work, and Jules will cover account-level communications. contact details to be shared.

[46:00] Aaron Chen: ok recap and owners — action items are in the notes; we'll follow up with the doc bundle. anything else?
[46:10] Samantha Liu: no that's it, thanks all.
[46:15] Mark Diaz: thanks, appreciate it.
[46:20] Jules Park: thanks everyone.

[46:45] Call ended.

References/Artifacts mentioned (links to be shared post-call):
- Kernel-selection trace (Priya to share)
- KV cache eviction histograms (Aaron / Priya)
- Synthetic workload test config (Priya)
- Draft exec postmortem deck (Jules)

End of transcript.
